sources.citation: Pelkey, Jamin R. 2011. A Phula Comparative Lexicon: Phola, Phuza, Muji, Phowa, Azha. SIL Language and Culture Documentation and Description 18. Dallas: SIL International.
sources.note: No Phala datapoint; Phala [ypa] named only in the subgrouping notes (p. 14: 'The Upriver Phula languages, Phola [ypg] and Phala [ypa], both feature TC-1 splits to /33/...'); 'stress'/'accent' occur 0 times.

sources.citation: Gonzalez Perez, Manuel David. 2022. Grammar, dimension and deixis in Phola, a Tibeto-Burman language of China. PhD thesis, Australian National University. xi+386 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a Harvard login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Describes Luodie PHOLA [ypg], not Phala. Sec. 3.1.4.4 'Stress and length' pp. 56-58: 'All lexically heavy monosyllables are stressed, and most polysyllabic words exhibit a distinctly stressed syllable as measured by intensity levels. Although not phonemic, stress influences segmental realisations' (grammatical particles encliticise and lack autonomous stress). Phala appears only as a closely related but poorly intelligible neighbour (pp. 12-13, 15, 21-22); nothing on Phala prosody.

sources.citation: Lama, Ziwo Qiu-Fuyuan. 2012. Subgrouping of Nisoic (Yi) languages. PhD diss., University of Texas at Arlington.
sources.note: No Phala datapoint ('Bola' there is the Burmish Bola of Dehong); nothing on Phala.
